group.title: Sayings and fixed phrases
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.lemma: actions speak louder than words
words.meaning: What people do shows more than what they say.
examples: He promised to help, but {actions speak louder than words}.
wrong: She said actions speak louder than words to show that promises matter most.

words.lemma: the early bird catches the worm
words.meaning: People who start early get the best chances.
examples: Get to the sale at eight: {the early bird catches the worm}.
wrong: He came last and quoted the early bird catches the worm.

words.lemma: don’t count your chickens before they hatch
words.meaning: Don’t rely on a good result before it actually happens.
examples: The deal isn’t signed yet, so {don’t count your chickens before they hatch}.
wrong: The money was already in her account, so he warned don’t count your chickens before they hatch.
words.ipa: /doʊnt kaʊnt jɔr ˈtʃɪkənz bɪˈfɔr ðeɪ hætʃ/

words.lemma: every cloud has a silver lining
words.meaning: Something good can come out of a bad situation.
examples: I lost my job but found a better one; {every cloud has a silver lining}.
wrong: Every cloud has a silver lining, he said, meaning good news always ends badly.

words.lemma: curiosity killed the cat
words.meaning: Being too interested in other people’s business can get you into trouble.
examples: Stop reading his letters; {curiosity killed the cat}.
wrong: Curiosity killed the cat means you should always ask more questions.

words.lemma: don’t judge a book by its cover
words.meaning: Don’t decide what something is like from how it looks.
examples: The cafe looks shabby, but {don’t judge a book by its cover}.
wrong: Don’t judge a book by its cover means first looks always tell the truth.
words.ipa: /doʊnt dʒʌdʒ ə bʊk baɪ ɪts ˈkʌvɚ/

words.lemma: where there’s smoke, there’s fire
words.meaning: If there are rumors, there is probably some truth in them.
examples: Nobody has proved it, but {where there’s smoke, there’s fire}.
wrong: Where there’s smoke, there’s fire means rumors are never true.

words.lemma: too many cooks spoil the broth
words.meaning: When too many people work on one thing, the result is worse.
examples: Ten people edited the report, and {too many cooks spoil the broth}.
wrong: Too many cooks spoil the broth, so let’s add more people to improve it.

words.lemma: the grass is always greener on the other side
words.meaning: Other people’s lives often seem better than yours, even when they are not.
examples: He wants my job and I want his; {the grass is always greener on the other side}.
wrong: The grass is always greener on the other side means you are happiest with what you have.
words.ipa: /ðə ɡræs ɪz ˈɔlweɪz ˈɡrinɚ ɑn ði ˈʌðɚ saɪd/

words.lemma: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
words.meaning: Something you already have is better than more you might not get.
examples: Take the offer now; {a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush}.
wrong: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, so refuse the sure offer and gamble.
words.ipa: /ə bɝd ɪn ðə hænd ɪz wɝθ tu ɪn ðə bʊʃ/

words.lemma: don’t put all your eggs in one basket
words.meaning: Don’t risk everything on one single plan.
examples: Invest in several funds: {don’t put all your eggs in one basket}.
wrong: Don’t put all your eggs in one basket, so spend all your savings on one stock.
words.ipa: /doʊnt pʊt ɔl jɔr ɛɡz ɪn wʌn ˈbæskɪt/

words.lemma: birds of a feather flock together
words.meaning: People who are alike tend to spend time together.
examples: All his friends love chess; {birds of a feather flock together}.
wrong: Birds of a feather flock together means opposites always become friends.

words.lemma: beggars can’t be choosers
words.meaning: When you need help, you must accept what is offered.
examples: It’s an old coat, but {beggars can’t be choosers}.
wrong: Beggars can’t be choosers means people in need should refuse anything less than the best.

words.lemma: you can’t have your cake and eat it too
words.meaning: You can’t keep the benefits of two things that exclude each other.
examples: You want a big house and no mortgage; {you can’t have your cake and eat it too}.
wrong: You can’t have your cake and eat it too means you can easily get both choices.
words.ipa: /ju kænt hæv jɔr keɪk ənd it ɪt tu/

words.lemma: it takes two to tango
words.meaning: Both people involved in a problem share the responsibility.
examples: Don’t blame only him for the fight; {it takes two to tango}.
wrong: It takes two to tango means only one person is ever to blame.

words.lemma: the pen is mightier than the sword
words.meaning: Writing and ideas have more power than violence.
examples: The journalist believed {the pen is mightier than the sword}.
wrong: The pen is mightier than the sword means armies always defeat ideas.
words.ipa: /ðə pɛn ɪz ˈmaɪtiɚ ðən ðə sɔrd/

words.lemma: necessity is the mother of invention
words.meaning: People find clever solutions when they really need them.
examples: With no tools, we used a spoon; {necessity is the mother of invention}.
wrong: Necessity is the mother of invention means people invent most when they need nothing.

words.lemma: absence makes the heart grow fonder
words.meaning: Being apart from someone makes you love them more.
examples: They live in different cities, but {absence makes the heart grow fonder}.
wrong: Absence makes the heart grow fonder means distance always kills love.

words.lemma: still waters run deep
words.meaning: Quiet people often have strong feelings or great knowledge.
examples: She rarely speaks, but {still waters run deep}.
wrong: Still waters run deep means quiet people have nothing inside.

words.lemma: strike while the iron is hot
words.meaning: Act quickly while you have a good chance.
examples: The client is interested now, so {strike while the iron is hot}.
wrong: Strike while the iron is hot, so wait a few months before you reply.

words.lemma: a stitch in time saves nine
words.meaning: Fixing a small problem early stops it becoming a big one.
examples: Repair that leak today; {a stitch in time saves nine}.
wrong: A stitch in time saves nine, so leave the crack until the wall falls down.

words.lemma: people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones
words.meaning: Don’t criticize others for faults that you have too.
examples: He calls me lazy, but {people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones}.
wrong: People who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones means you should criticize others for your own faults.
words.ipa: /ˈpipəl hu lɪv ɪn ɡlæs ˈhaʊzɪz ˈʃʊdənt θroʊ stoʊnz/

words.lemma: the pot calling the kettle black
words.meaning: Someone criticizing another person for a fault they also have.
examples: Him calling me late is {the pot calling the kettle black}.
wrong: It was the pot calling the kettle black when a punctual man praised another for being on time.

words.lemma: Rome wasn’t built in a day
words.meaning: Big, important things take a long time to do.
examples: Learning a language takes years; {Rome wasn’t built in a day}.
wrong: Rome wasn’t built in a day, so expect to master the piano by Friday.

words.lemma: you can lead a horse to water
words.meaning: You can give someone a chance, but you can’t force them to take it.
examples: I gave him the books, but {you can lead a horse to water}.
wrong: You can lead a horse to water means you can always force people to do things.
words.ipa: /ju kæn lid ə hɔrs tə ˈwɔtɚ/

words.lemma: all that glitters is not gold
words.meaning: Things that look attractive are not always good or valuable.
examples: The offer looks amazing, but {all that glitters is not gold}.
wrong: All that glitters is not gold means shiny things are always valuable.

words.lemma: don’t bite the hand that feeds you
words.meaning: Don’t be unkind to the person who helps or supports you.
examples: Insulting your sponsor is silly; {don’t bite the hand that feeds you}.
wrong: Don’t bite the hand that feeds you means you should attack the people who support you.
words.ipa: /doʊnt baɪt ðə hænd ðæt fidz ju/

words.lemma: a watched pot never boils
words.meaning: Waiting for something feels slower when you keep checking it.
examples: Stop refreshing your email; {a watched pot never boils}.
wrong: A watched pot never boils means time goes faster when you stare at the clock.

words.lemma: once bitten, twice shy
words.meaning: After a bad experience, you are more careful the next time.
examples: After that scam, she checks everything; {once bitten, twice shy}.
wrong: Once bitten, twice shy, he said, and repeated the same mistake without a thought.

words.lemma: there’s no such thing as a free lunch
words.meaning: Anything that seems free usually has a hidden cost.
examples: The free phone comes with a long contract; {there’s no such thing as a free lunch}.
wrong: There’s no such thing as a free lunch means free offers never have conditions.
words.ipa: /ðɛrz noʊ sʌtʃ θɪŋ æz ə fri lʌntʃ/

words.lemma: two wrongs don’t make a right
words.meaning: Doing something bad back to someone does not fix things.
examples: He lied to you, but {two wrongs don’t make a right}.
wrong: Two wrongs don’t make a right, so get revenge for every insult.

words.lemma: let bygones be bygones
words.meaning: To forget past quarrels and be friendly again.
examples: It was years ago; let’s {let bygones be bygones}.
wrong: They let bygones be bygones and argued about the old quarrel every day.

words.lemma: out of sight, out of mind
words.meaning: People soon forget things or people they no longer see.
examples: I put the cake in the cupboard: {out of sight, out of mind}.
wrong: Out of sight, out of mind means we think most about what we never see.

words.lemma: the squeaky wheel gets the grease
words.meaning: People who complain loudly usually get attention first.
examples: She called them every day; {the squeaky wheel gets the grease}.
wrong: The squeaky wheel gets the grease, so the quietest customer was served first.

words.lemma: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure
words.meaning: Stopping a problem early is easier than fixing it later.
examples: Get a checkup now; {an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure}.
wrong: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, so wait until you are seriously ill.
words.ipa: /ən aʊns əv prɪˈvɛnʃən ɪz wɝθ ə paʊnd əv kjʊr/

words.lemma: part and parcel
words.meaning: A basic, natural part of something that cannot be avoided.
examples: Travel is {part and parcel} of the job.
wrong: Long hours are part and parcel of the job, so they never happen.

words.lemma: few and far between
words.meaning: Very rare; not happening or found often.
examples: Good jobs here are {few and far between}.
wrong: Cafes are few and far between here; there is one on every corner.

words.lemma: touch and go
words.meaning: Very uncertain, especially about whether something bad will happen.
examples: It was {touch and go} whether the plane would land safely.
wrong: It was touch and go, as the result was certain from the start.

words.lemma: neither here nor there
words.meaning: Not important or not connected to the matter being discussed.
examples: What he earns is {neither here nor there}; is he a good worker?
wrong: His age is neither here nor there, so it is the main point of the case.

words.lemma: the be-all and end-all
words.meaning: The most important thing of all.
examples: Money isn’t {the be-all and end-all}.
wrong: For her, music is the be-all and end-all, so she hardly cares about it.
